title: Didactic example — visual intro to Fourier transforms
description: A didactic walkthrough framed around 3Blue1Brown's "But what is a Fourier Transform" video. Demonstrates how the Video widget plus a transcript with click-to-seek lets a tutor scaffold a video lesson with reading material around it.

data.markdown:
## What you're about to watch

The Fourier transform decomposes a signal — a sound, an image, a time series — into a sum of pure sine waves of different frequencies. It is the foundation of:

- Audio compression (MP3, AAC).
- Image compression (JPEG's discrete cosine transform).
- Signal processing of every kind — filtering, equalisation, denoising.
- Quantum mechanics, where the position/momentum representations are Fourier conjugates.

The video below is a **visual** introduction — Grant Sanderson winds the signal around a circle and shows the centre-of-mass argument that motivates the integral.

:::callout{type="info" title="How to use this lesson"}
Click any line in the transcript to jump the player to that moment. Use it as a navigable table of contents — the video is 21 minutes but the Q&A in the transcript sections is the part most students rewatch.
:::

sections.title: But what is a Fourier transform?

data.title: But what is a Fourier transform? — 3Blue1Brown

transcript.text: A friend of mine recently asked me whether I knew of any nice intuitions for the Fourier transform.
transcript.speaker: Grant

transcript.text: We're going to develop the Fourier transform from a more general principle: winding a signal around a circle.
Imagine a pure cosine wave at frequency 3 hertz — the height of the wave over time looks like this.
Now wind that signal around the origin — multiply each sample's complex value by e^(-2πift) for some winding frequency f.
When the winding frequency matches the signal's frequency, the wound-up signal is lopsided — its centre of mass is shifted away from the origin.
When the winding frequency does NOT match, the wound-up signal is balanced around the origin and the centre of mass is roughly zero.
So plotting centre-of-mass (as a complex number) against winding frequency reveals which frequencies are present in the signal — that's the Fourier transform.
Up to a constant factor, this matches the textbook integral definition: F(f) = ∫ x(t) e^(-2πift) dt.
Two key takeaways: (1) the transform is linear in the signal, and (2) shifts in time become phase rotations in frequency.
The discrete version — the DFT — is what every fast Fourier transform algorithm computes; FFT is just an O(n log n) way to multiply the same matrix.

data.markdown:
## Things to think about

After watching, ask yourself:

1. Why does winding at the matching frequency make the centre of mass non-zero?
2. What does a *real* signal (only cosines, no sines) imply about the symmetry of its Fourier transform?
3. How does the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) relate to the continuous integral?
4. Why is the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) $O(n \log n)$ instead of the naive $O(n^{2})$?
